What if the universe has been hiding a cosmic surprise right under our noses? For decades, astronomers have been scouring the Milky Way in search of elusive black holes, those mysterious objects where not even light escapes. But now, a daring theory suggests that some of these black holes might actually be something even stranger: hidden wormholes! Get ready for a fascinating journey into the heart of cosmic enigmas.

The Challenge of Detecting Black Holes

Detecting black holes isn’t exactly a walk in the park. In fact, the few black holes spotted in our galaxy, the Milky Way, are only observed indirectly. Typically, they’re surrounded by a superheated accretion disk that emits copious amounts of X-rays—basically, the cosmic equivalent of a neon sign flashing “Black hole here!” Still, plenty of black holes out there remain invisible, possibly only betraying their presence through the rare phenomenon of gravitational lensing. But just how many black holes are lurking in our galaxy? A group of astrophysicists thinks they’ve uncovered the answer—and it’s nothing short of staggering!

From Quasars to Einstein: Sixty Years of Black Hole Curiosity

It’s been roughly 60 years since the scientific community started taking the concept of black holes and their existence in the observable universe seriously. Experimentally, the discovery of quasars played a crucial role. On the theoretical front, Roger Penrose’s research was pivotal in shifting ideas about these objects, which had been predicted by Einstein’s general theory of relativity.

Let’s quickly recall: a black hole is defined by the existence of an event horizon, a closed surface marking a region of space-time from which nothing can escape—not unless you can travel faster than the speed of light (spoiler: you can’t). We still have no idea what state matter and space-time take inside a black hole. Scientists suspect that not only quantum gravitational effects come into play, but also possible tweaks to the equations of Einstein’s theory itself. Such modifications could change the theory’s prediction of a singularity at the heart of known black hole solutions—if the theory operates on its own, that is.

Black Holes, Wormholes, and Mind-Bending Possibilities

Black hole theory can be tested—and challenged—by both gravitational waves and the images of the event horizon’s shadow, as well as by exploring alternatives to general relativity itself. For years, some black hole theorists have suspected that the objects we observe in astrophysics as black holes might actually be wormholes: those legendary bridges through space-time, perhaps allowing for rapid travel between stars. Efforts to unlock this cosmic conundrum include observations with the Russian space telescope RadioAstron as well as the Event Horizon Telescope.

Here’s a neat twist. Almost 20 years ago, physicists Thibault Damour and Sergey Solodukhin stated in a paper on arXiv:

“Surprisingly, many of the properties considered ‘characteristic’ of a black hole (endowed with an event horizon) can be faithfully imitated by a globally static wormhole, lacking an event horizon. This includes apparently irreversible accretion of matter, the so-called ‘no-hair’ properties, quasi-normal mode oscillations, and even the dissipative properties of black hole horizons, such as a finite surface resistivity equal to 377 ohms. The only way to distinguish these two geometries within a reasonable observation time would be to detect Hawking radiation; however, this is far too weak to be of practical interest in the case of astrophysical black holes.”

To date, we trust Einstein’s relativistic theory of gravitation more than ever, as well as the reality of black holes. Yet, the scientific community stays open-minded—especially with emerging ideas like the theory of entangled relativity. The exploration of this theory is just beginning, but it already stands as a particular type of so-called tensor-scalar theory, which aims to go beyond Einstein’s general relativity.

Of course, black holes became especially famous thanks to the work and writings of Stephen Hawking. The astronomy of gravitational waves—celebrating its tenth birthday in September 2025—continues to deliver remarkable evidence supporting Hawking’s insights.

Yet, if black holes really are wormholes, this mind-bending realization would fit right in with science fiction, such as Joe Haldeman’s celebrated 1974 novel The Forever War.
